records.sourceFile: Strength and power thresholds to identify high and low linear sprint speed performers in collegiate American football players.pdf

paper.citation: Philipp NM, Crawford DA, Cabarkapa D, Fry AC. Strength and Power Thresholds to Identify High and Low Linear Sprint Speed Performers in Collegiate American Football Players. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(1):74-79.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional classification study evaluated strength and power thresholds associated with faster and slower 40-yard-dash performance in collegiate American football players grouped by body mass.
paper.tldr: Vertical and broad jumps best distinguished faster from slower 40-yard-dash performers in 294 collegiate football players, while relative hang clean and squat added group-specific information. The cut points are roster-specific classification references, not universal speed prescriptions.
paper.methods: Researchers analyzed 294 NCAA football players and divided them into high-body-mass and low-body-mass groups of 147 athletes each. Players completed a hand-timed 40-yard dash, vertical and broad jumps, and relative 3-repetition-maximum strength and power tests. Median splits defined faster and slower groups, and receiver-operating-characteristic and logistic-regression analyses quantified discrimination and thresholds.
paper.findings: Areas under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve ranged from 0.695 to 0.903. In the high-body-mass group, vertical jump had an AUC of 0.903, broad jump 0.883, and relative hang clean 0.848. In the low-body-mass group, vertical jump had an AUC of 0.779, broad jump 0.753, and relative squat 0.740. Threshold values varied by body-mass group and test.
paper.limitations: The study was cross-sectional and used a median split, hand timing, jump-mat measures, and 3-repetition-maximum lifts. Nutrition and hydration were not controlled, and the male collegiate-football thresholds were not tested prospectively or in an external roster.
paper.practicalImplications: Use jump and relative-strength results as supporting context when profiling speed qualities within comparable position and body-mass groups. Build local reference distributions and validate any cut points against the program's own timing and testing methods before using them in decisions.
paper.athleteDev: Show athletes how relative force and power qualities relate to sprint profiles without turning one threshold into a label. Pair test results with technical sprint observation, training history, position demands, and repeat testing.
paper.rtp: These thresholds were derived from healthy players and are not return-to-sport criteria. During reconditioning, compare the athlete with preinjury and position-relevant trends while restoring sprint exposure and task tolerance progressively.

records.sourceFile: The Effects of Sleep Extension on the Athletic Performance of Collegiate Basketball Players.pdf

paper.citation: Mah CD, Mah KE, Kezirian EJ, Dement WC. The Effects of Sleep Extension on the Athletic Performance of Collegiate Basketball Players. Sleep. 2011;34(7):943-950.
paper.abstract: This uncontrolled pre-post study examined whether extending sleep opportunity affected sport performance, vigilance, sleepiness, and mood in men's collegiate basketball players.
paper.tldr: Eleven collegiate basketball players slept about 111 minutes longer and improved sprint, shooting, vigilance, sleepiness, and mood measures during a sleep-extension phase. Because the study lacked a control group, it supports correcting sleep insufficiency but cannot isolate sleep as the cause of every change.
paper.methods: Eleven healthy Stanford men's varsity basketball players completed a 2- to 4-week habitual-sleep baseline and then 5 to 7 weeks of sleep extension with a goal of at least 10 hours in bed each night. Wrist actigraphy, sleep logs, a timed sprint, free throws, three-point shots, psychomotor vigilance, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, and mood measures were collected repeatedly.
paper.findings: Objective sleep duration increased by 110.9 plus or minus 79.7 minutes. Mean sprint time improved from 16.2 to 15.5 seconds, free-throw accuracy increased by 9 percentage points, and three-point accuracy increased by 9.2 percentage points. Psychomotor vigilance, daytime sleepiness, and mood also improved during the extension phase.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, male, and drawn from one team, with no randomization, crossover, or concurrent control. Season progression, practice exposure, expectancy, and repayment of accumulated sleep debt could have influenced the outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: When an athlete is habitually undersleeping, create more sleep opportunity and monitor actual sleep, alertness, mood, and performance over several weeks. Set schedules around individual sleep need rather than treating 10 hours in bed as a mandatory universal dose.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to recognize chronic sleep restriction and to plan bedtime, wake time, travel, study, and recovery routines. Use repeated data to connect sleep opportunity with how the athlete feels and performs.
paper.rtp: Adequate sleep supports recovery and learning during rehabilitation, but improved alertness does not equal restored tissue capacity. Integrate sleep support with medical criteria, progressive loading, and task-specific reconditioning.

records.sourceFile: Elite North American soccer performance in thermally challenging environments  - An explorative approach to tracking outcomes.pdf

paper.citation: Draper G, Atkinson G, Chesterton P, Portas M, Wright M. Elite North American Soccer Performance in Thermally Challenging Environments: An Explorative Approach to Tracking Outcomes. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2023;41(11):1107-1114.
paper.abstract: This longitudinal observational study explored associations between environmental heat measures, match-running output, and differential perceived exertion in elite North American soccer.
paper.tldr: Across four seasons, hotter conditions had mostly trivial-to-small associations with elite soccer running outputs, including small reductions in high-speed running and a small increase in breathlessness RPE. Environmental heat is useful context, not a stand-alone predictor of match demand.
paper.methods: Thirty-seven elite male soccer players contributed between 3 and 98 match observations across four North American seasons. GPS-derived total and high-speed distance and differential ratings of perceived exertion were paired with kickoff temperature, weekly temperature change, and heat index. Within-player general linear models and repeated-measures correlations estimated associations.
paper.findings: Associations between thermal variables and total distance were trivial to small. Higher temperature and heat index were associated with small reductions in high-speed running, with correlations of approximately -0.17 to -0.14 for most thermal measures. Heat index also had a small positive relationship with breathlessness RPE, while other perceptual associations were limited.
paper.limitations: Players contributed unequal numbers of matches, and wet-bulb globe temperature was unavailable. The models could not fully account for fixture congestion, substitutions, tactics, travel, hydration, cooling, or individual acclimatization.
paper.practicalImplications: Add heat and heat index to match-context dashboards and compare each athlete's output and perceptual response with similar exposures. Use the signal alongside role, minutes, tactics, travel, and recovery status when planning hydration, cooling, substitutions, and subsequent training.
paper.athleteDev: Help athletes develop individualized heat plans through practice exposures, hydration and cooling routines, and postmatch review. Emphasize that perceived breathing strain and external output may respond differently.
paper.rtp: During return to competition in hot conditions, progress environmental and match demands together. A small group-average temperature effect does not replace symptom monitoring, medical judgment, or individual heat-tolerance assessment.

records.sourceFile: Evaluating the relationship between neurological function, neuromuscular fatigue, and subjective performance measures in professional rugby union players.pdf

paper.citation: Daly E, Pearce AJ, Esser P, Ryan L. Evaluating the Relationship Between Neurological Function, Neuromuscular Fatigue, and Subjective Performance Measures in Professional Rugby Union Players. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2022;4:1058326.
paper.abstract: This professional rugby case series evaluated relationships among neurological, autonomic, neuromuscular, mood, and injury-status measures collected repeatedly during the competitive season.
paper.tldr: Neurological, neuromuscular, autonomic, and subjective readiness measures in 11 professional rugby players were largely nonredundant; reactive strength had only a weak association with direct-current potential. The results favor a multi-signal review over one proprietary readiness score.
paper.methods: Eleven male senior professional rugby union players were tested three times per week for six weeks during midseason. Measures included Omegawave direct-current potential and heart-rate-variability outputs, countermovement-jump reactive strength index modified, Profile of Mood States, and injury status. Repeated observations were examined for relationships among measures.
paper.findings: Reactive strength index modified and direct-current potential had a weak negative correlation of r = -0.17. The broader neurological, autonomic, neuromuscular, and subjective measures showed limited convergence, suggesting that they reflected different aspects of player status rather than one interchangeable readiness construct.
paper.limitations: The case series involved 11 male players in one professional environment over six weeks and had no control group. A proprietary system generated neurological values, and the study did not establish prospective injury prediction, decision thresholds, or long-term validity.
paper.practicalImplications: Review readiness signals together and investigate meaningful within-athlete deviations rather than expecting one metric to summarize the athlete. Document the decision rule, repeatability, context, and action linked to each measure before it enters daily practice.
paper.athleteDev: Use monitoring conversations to build athlete self-awareness and reporting trust. Explain what each measure can and cannot indicate so athletes do not interpret a single low score as proof of fatigue or injury.
paper.rtp: A multi-domain dashboard can support reconditioning review, but none of these measures is a clearance test. Return decisions still require clinical status, progressive exposure, function, and sport-specific tolerance.

records.sourceFile: The Sprint Mechanics Assessment Score - A qualitative screening tool for the in-field assessment of sprint running mechanics.pdf

paper.citation: Bramah C, Tawiah-Dodoo J, Rhodes S, Elliott JD, Dos'Santos T. The Sprint Mechanics Assessment Score: A Qualitative Screening Tool for the In-field Assessment of Sprint Running Mechanics. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2024;52(6):1608-1616.
paper.abstract: This methodological study developed and tested the rater reliability of a 12-item field-based qualitative score for maximum-velocity sprint mechanics in elite soccer players.
paper.tldr: The 12-item Sprint Mechanics Assessment Score showed good within- and between-rater reliability on elite soccer sprint video, with a 1-point standard error. It can structure observation, but reliability does not establish injury prediction or coaching effectiveness.
paper.methods: Maximum 35-m sprint videos from 136 elite soccer players were scored using the 12-item Sprint Mechanics Assessment Score. A balanced subgroup of 36 players, 18 men and 18 women, was rescored to assess intrarater and interrater reliability with intraclass correlations, standard error of measurement, and item-level agreement.
paper.findings: Intrarater reliability was good with an ICC of 0.828 and interrater reliability was good with an ICC of 0.799; both had a standard error of measurement of 1 point. Item agreement ranged from 75.0% to 88.8% within raters and 66.6% to 88.8% between raters. Overall scores did not differ by sex.
paper.limitations: The study established reliability only. It used a single sprint trial and assessors familiar with the method, and it did not test prospective injury risk, sensitivity to intervention, novice-rater performance, or transfer beyond elite soccer.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the score as a repeatable vocabulary for reviewing sprint video and prioritizing a deeper technical assessment. Account for the 1-point measurement error and avoid acting on isolated item changes without repeat observation and performance context.
paper.athleteDev: Pair video and the score with athlete-friendly technical feedback, one or two trainable priorities, and repeat trials. Preserve individual solutions instead of treating every flagged item as a fault that must be standardized.
paper.rtp: The score may help document sprint-mechanics progression after injury, but it is not a validated injury-risk or clearance tool. Combine it with symptoms, capacity, exposure, speed, and sport-task tolerance.

records.sourceFile: Validating InBody 570 multi-frequency bioelectrical   impedance analyzer vs DXA for body fat percentage analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Miller RM, Chambers TL, Burns SP. Validating InBody 570 Multi-frequency Bioelectrical Impedance Analyzer Versus DXA for Body Fat Percentage Analysis. Journal of Exercise Physiology Online. 2016;19(5):71-78.
paper.abstract: This validation study compared body-fat percentage from the InBody 570 multifrequency bioelectrical impedance analyzer with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry in recreationally active university adults.
paper.tldr: InBody 570 and DXA body-fat percentages were strongly correlated in 110 young adults, but InBody averaged 4.62 percentage points lower. The devices should not be treated as interchangeable for absolute body-fat values.
paper.methods: Seventy-two men and 38 women aged 18 to 25 years completed InBody 570 and DXA assessment during the same visit after instructions to fast for 12 hours, avoid exercise for 12 hours, and avoid alcohol for 24 hours. Correlations, shared variance, and mean differences were calculated for the full sample and sex subgroups.
paper.findings: InBody and DXA body-fat percentages correlated at r = 0.94, representing 88% shared variance. Mean body-fat percentage was 25.61% by DXA and 20.99% by InBody, and the overall and subgroup method differences were statistically significant at P less than .0001.
paper.limitations: Correlation measures association rather than agreement, and the report did not provide a Bland-Altman analysis. The sample was young and recreationally active, preparation compliance was self-reported, hydration was not objectively verified, and results are specific to the tested device and algorithm.
paper.practicalImplications: For longitudinal monitoring, standardize preparation, time of day, device, and operator and interpret change against normal device error. Do not compare an athlete's InBody percentage directly with a DXA percentage as though they share the same scale.
paper.athleteDev: Frame body-composition data as one imperfect monitoring input, protect athlete privacy, and avoid value judgments around a single percentage. Focus feedback on health, fueling, training, and meaningful trends.
paper.rtp: Body-fat percentage is not a general return-to-sport criterion. If composition monitoring is medically relevant, use consistent methods and integrate the result with clinical, nutrition, and functional information.

records.sourceFile: Adverse Effects of Anabolic Androgenic Steroid Abuse in Athletes and Physically Active Individuals - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Liu M, Yu Y. Adverse Effects of Anabolic Androgenic Steroid Abuse in Athletes and Physically Active Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Substance Use and Misuse. 2025;60(6):873-887.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified cardiovascular, hepatic, lipid, and endocrine differences associated with anabolic-androgenic steroid abuse in athletes and physically active individuals.
paper.tldr: Anabolic-androgenic steroid abuse was associated with meaningfully higher blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, and liver enzymes and lower testosterone. Heterogeneous observational exposure evidence supports medical concern but cannot predict an individual athlete's exact effect.
paper.methods: The authors systematically identified studies comparing athletes or physically active anabolic-androgenic steroid users with nonusers and pooled continuous cardiometabolic, hepatic, and endocrine outcomes. Random-effects analyses generated weighted mean differences and 95% confidence intervals, with study quality and publication-bias considerations reported.
paper.findings: Steroid abuse was associated with systolic blood pressure 12.43 mmHg higher, 95% CI 9.59 to 15.26; diastolic pressure 8.09 mmHg higher, 95% CI 5.62 to 10.57; LDL cholesterol 9.12 mg/dL higher; AST 14.47 U/L higher; ALT 12.16 U/L higher; and testosterone 141.57 ng/dL lower than comparison groups.
paper.limitations: Studies varied in quality, steroid type, dose, duration, co-use, and outcome assessment and were vulnerable to selection and publication bias. Most exposure evidence was observational, and unmeasured polysubstance use and comorbidities limit causal and individual-level interpretation.
paper.practicalImplications: Provide confidential, nonpunitive screening and education about cardiovascular, hepatic, endocrine, and mental-health risks. Abnormal history, symptoms, blood pressure, or laboratory findings should trigger appropriate medical assessment rather than performance-staff diagnosis.
paper.athleteDev: Build supplement and drug literacy, explain that appearance and short-term performance do not indicate safety, and make help-seeking pathways clear. Avoid stigma that discourages honest disclosure.
paper.rtp: Athletes with suspected adverse effects need clinician-led evaluation and individualized activity decisions. Normalization of one marker does not by itself establish recovery or readiness for unrestricted training.

records.sourceFile: Association of Lower Limb Compression Garments During HighIntensity Exercise with Performance and Physiological Responses- A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: da Silva CA, Helal L, da Silva RP, Belli KC, Umpierre D, Stein R. Association of Lower Limb Compression Garments During High-Intensity Exercise With Performance and Physiological Responses: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(8):1859-1873.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether lower-limb compression garments worn during high-intensity exercise improve performance or physiological and perceptual responses.
paper.tldr: Across 23 randomized trials, lower-limb compression garments worn during intense exercise did not meaningfully improve running, jumping, oxygen uptake, lactate, or perceived exertion. Comfort or recovery preferences should be separated from acute performance claims.
paper.methods: The review included 23 randomized controlled trials in athletes and physically active adults. Meta-analyses compared compression garments with control conditions for running performance across distances, vertical jump, maximal and submaximal oxygen uptake, blood lactate, and rating of perceived exertion.
paper.findings: No meaningful benefit was found for the pooled performance or physiological outcomes. The weighted mean difference for 50- to 400-m running was 0.06 seconds, 95% CI -1.99 to 2.11, and the pooled RPE difference was -0.20 units, 95% CI -0.48 to 0.08. Heterogeneity was generally low.
paper.limitations: Several trials incompletely reported randomization and allocation. Garment pressure, exercise protocols, and running distances varied; some analyses shared control groups, and the evidence focused on garments worn during exercise rather than every possible postexercise recovery use.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not allocate training or competition resources on the assumption that lower-limb compression garments reliably enhance acute high-intensity performance. If athletes prefer them, assess comfort, fit, cost, and the separate evidence for the intended recovery use.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to distinguish plausible mechanisms and marketing claims from demonstrated performance effects. An individual preference can be respected without presenting it as a proven ergogenic aid.
paper.rtp: Compression garments are not a substitute for progressive loading, symptom monitoring, or objective function. Any use during rehabilitation should be tied to a specific comfort or clinical purpose rather than presumed performance restoration.

records.sourceFile: Athlete Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators Abuse - A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Vasireddi N, Hahamyan HA, Gould HP, Gregory AJM, Gausden EB, Dodson CC, Voos JE, Calcei JG. Athlete Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators Abuse: A Systematic Review. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;53(4):999-1009.
paper.abstract: This systematic review synthesized athlete SARM use, potential performance effects, adverse outcomes, and the reliability of products marketed as selective androgen receptor modulators.
paper.tldr: The SARM literature suggests low but uncertain athlete use, possible lean-mass effects, serious hepatic and other safety concerns, and frequent mismatch between product labels and contents. No SARM is approved for athlete performance use.
paper.methods: The review included 72 articles published from 2003 through 2022, spanning prevalence surveys, clinical and preclinical studies, product analyses, and case reports. Thirteen case reports described 15 men, including eight athletes, with a median age of 32 years and a mean reported oral exposure of eight weeks.
paper.findings: Available athlete surveys estimated SARM use at approximately 1% to 3%. The literature described possible lean-mass and performance-related effects alongside hepatic, cardiovascular, endocrine, and tendon concerns. Online products were often contaminated, mislabeled, or supplied at doses above those studied clinically.
paper.limitations: Study designs and outcomes were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis. Only four SARMs were emphasized, case reports and co-supplementation prevent causal attribution, abstracts were excluded, and the prevalence evidence was limited and vulnerable to underreporting.
paper.practicalImplications: Ask explicitly about SARMs and internet-purchased supplements during health and nutrition reviews. Treat the product label as unreliable, reinforce anti-doping implications, and direct symptoms or use disclosures to qualified medical care.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes that selective marketing does not mean tissue-selective safety and that an unapproved product can contain undeclared drugs. Make confidential disclosure and help-seeking easier than concealment.
paper.rtp: Potential hepatic, cardiovascular, endocrine, or tendon effects require clinician-led evaluation. Stopping use or feeling better is not by itself sufficient evidence for unrestricted return.

records.sourceFile: Biomechanical Determinants of Change of Direction Performance - A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Singh U, Leicht AS, Connor JD, Brice SM, Alves A, Doma K. Biomechanical Determinants of Change of Direction Performance: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2025;55(9):2207-2224.
paper.abstract: This systematic review synthesized biomechanical variables associated with faster preplanned change-of-direction performance across different cutting angles.
paper.tldr: Faster change of direction was associated with shorter contact, greater approach and exit speed, stronger braking and propulsion, lower center of mass, and task-specific trunk and joint mechanics. These correlates vary by angle and do not establish one universal causal technique.
paper.methods: Thirteen studies involving 374 participants were reviewed, with methodological quality scores ranging from 73% to 96%. Studies examined preplanned 45- to 180-degree change-of-direction tasks and related completion time or velocity to ground-contact, force, center-of-mass, trunk, joint-moment, power, and kinematic variables.
paper.findings: Faster performance was commonly associated with shorter ground-contact time, higher approach and exit velocity, greater braking and propulsive forces, greater trunk inclination, a lower center of mass, and larger task-specific lower-limb moments and power. The relevant strategy changed with cut angle and task constraints.
paper.limitations: The evidence was correlational, tasks and timing methods were heterogeneous, and 79.4% of participants were male. No included study examined unplanned or reactive change of direction, and sex-, sport-, and training-status moderation were poorly resolved.
paper.practicalImplications: Profile change-of-direction tasks by angle, approach speed, braking demand, exit objective, and decision component. Coach the athlete's limiting strategy and retest the same task rather than applying one technical cue across every cut.
paper.athleteDev: Develop braking capacity, reacceleration, trunk control, and perception-action skill progressively. Use video and force information to help athletes understand tradeoffs between speed, control, and joint loading.
paper.rtp: Progress from planned to increasingly reactive and sport-specific cuts while monitoring symptoms, speed, braking exposure, and movement strategy. Cross-sectional biomechanical correlates are not clearance thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Blood flow-restricted training for  lower extremity muscle weakness due to knee pathology - A systematic  review.pdf

paper.citation: Barber-Westin S, Noyes FR. Blood Flow-Restricted Training for Lower Extremity Muscle Weakness Due to Knee Pathology: A Systematic Review. Sports Health. 2019;11(1):69-83.
paper.abstract: This systematic review evaluated blood-flow-restricted training for lower-extremity weakness in patients with ACL reconstruction, knee arthroscopy, osteoarthritis, or patellofemoral pain.
paper.tldr: Blood-flow-restricted exercise improved strength in six of seven controlled knee-rehabilitation studies, but protocols were heterogeneous and evidence for hypertrophy, hamstrings, and safety was less complete. Use it as a supervised load-management option, not a universal replacement for heavy resistance training.
paper.methods: Nine controlled studies, eight level 1 and one level 2, included 165 patients and 170 control participants with ACL reconstruction, knee arthroscopy, knee osteoarthritis, or patellofemoral pain. The review compared blood-flow-restricted protocols with conventional rehabilitation for strength, muscle size, function, and reported complications.
paper.findings: Six of seven studies that measured strength reported significant benefit from blood-flow-restricted training. Some studies reported quadriceps cross-sectional-area gains, while only two addressed hamstring outcomes. No training complications were reported in the included studies.
paper.limitations: Studies were small and differed in knee pathology, cuff system, pressure, load, duration, and comparator. Most evidence concerned quadriceps strength, significance was not consistently linked to minimal clinically important change, and zero reported complications cannot establish safety across broader populations.
paper.practicalImplications: Consider blood-flow-restricted exercise when pain, healing status, or joint tolerance limits heavy loading. Screen contraindications, use individualized occlusion pressure and trained supervision, and progress toward conventional resistance and functional loading as tolerance allows.
paper.athleteDev: Explain the purpose, expected discomfort, safety checks, and progression criteria before use. The method should expand the athlete's loading options while preserving confidence in the longer rehabilitation plan.
paper.rtp: Improved strength under blood-flow restriction is one rehabilitation input, not proof of sport readiness. Restore unrestricted strength, rate of force, movement, running, and sport exposure before clearance.

records.sourceFile: Can caffeine change the game - Effects of acute caffeine intake on specific performance in intermittent sports during competition - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Diaz-Lara J, Nieto-Acevedo R, Abian-Vicen J, Del Coso J. Can Caffeine Change the Game? Effects of Acute Caffeine Intake on Specific Performance in Intermittent Sports During Competition: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2024;19(11):1180-1196.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated acute caffeine effects on competition-specific actions and external-load outcomes in intermittent team, racket, and combat sports.
paper.tldr: Across 24 double-blind crossover studies, acute caffeine produced small-to-moderate increases in several intermittent-sport actions, including sprints, accelerations, decelerations, impacts, offensive efforts, and successful actions. Individual response and sleep or side-effect costs still require trialing.
paper.methods: Twenty-four double-blind randomized crossover studies included 399 participants, 264 male and 135 female, from team, racket, and combat sports. Caffeine doses were generally about 3 to 6.4 mg/kg, and meta-analyses pooled competition or competition-like counts of sprints, impacts, accelerations, decelerations, offensive actions, and successful sport-specific efforts.
paper.findings: Caffeine increased sprints with an SMD of 0.48, impacts 0.28, accelerations 0.35, decelerations 0.63, offensive efforts 0.36, and successful actions 0.44. Effects were not uniform across every sport or outcome and represent acute group-average responses.
paper.limitations: Sports, caffeine forms, timing, doses, and outcome definitions varied. Only two studies checked blinding, while habitual caffeine use, expectancy, adverse effects, sex-specific response, and the effect of late-day intake on sleep were inconsistently assessed.
paper.practicalImplications: Trial caffeine in training with the exact competition timing, food, hydration, and sleep context. Start near the lower end of effective dosing, record benefit and adverse response, and avoid assuming more caffeine produces more performance.
paper.athleteDev: Teach dose literacy, product verification, and the tradeoff between an acute stimulus and later sleep. Athletes should have a rehearsed plan and a clear option not to use caffeine.
paper.rtp: Caffeine may alter alertness and output but does not restore tissue capacity or substitute for graded exposure. During return to sport, avoid using stimulation to mask symptoms or exceed the planned workload.
